questions.stem: Which amino acid is most likely to act as a proton donor/acceptor in an enzyme active site at physiological pH?
questions.explanation: Histidine's imidazole pKa (~6) lets it switch between protonated and unprotonated states at pH 7.4. B: Lysine (pKa ~10.5) stays protonated. C: Arginine (pKa ~12.5) is always positive. D: Leucine is nonpolar. E: Glycine has no ionizable side chain.

questions.stem: Proline and glycine both destabilize an α helix, but for different reasons. Why does glycine do so?

options.A: Its rigid ring introduces a kink
options.B: Its bulky side chain clashes with neighbors
options.C: Its charge opposes the helix dipole

questions.explanation: Glycine's side chain is only a hydrogen, so it is unusually flexible and coiling it into a helix is unfavorable. A: The rigid ring and kink describe proline, the helix breaker. B: Glycine has the smallest side chain. C: Glycine's side chain is uncharged. D: Cysteine forms disulfides.

questions.stem: A lab estimates protein concentration in a sample by measuring absorbance at 280 nm. Which residues mainly produce this signal?
questions.explanation: Trp and Tyr absorb strongly at 280 nm. A: Phe absorbs weakly (~257 nm) and leucine not at all. B: Sulfur residues aren't the basis. C: Basic residues don't absorb at 280 nm. E: Neither absorbs at 280 nm.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes the disease-causing prion protein (PrPSc) from normal PrPC?
questions.explanation: PrPSc has the same sequence as PrPC but a β-sheet-rich, insoluble, protease-resistant conformation that templates conversion of PrPC. A, D: The sequence is identical. B: This describes normal PrPC. E: PrPSc is refolded, not unstructured.

questions.stem: Which chaperone binds exposed hydrophobic patches on a nascent polypeptide, keeping it unfolded until synthesis is complete?
questions.explanation: Hsp70 (with Hsp40) holds nascent chains unfolded and prevents aggregation until synthesis is complete. B: The proteasome degrades proteins. C: Ubiquitin tags misfolded proteins for degradation. D: SRP targets ribosomes to the ER. E: Chaperonins form a barrel-shaped protected chamber in which the protein folds.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus over 5 months; MRI shows cortical diffusion restriction. At autopsy, the brain shows spongiform change. What is the pathogenic mechanism?

options.B: Trinucleotide repeat expansion in a nuclear gene
options.D: Misfolded protein that converts normal protein to its β-sheet form

questions.explanation: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease: PrPSc templates PrPC conversion to a β-sheet, protease-resistant form. A: Tau tangles are Alzheimer disease. B: Repeat expansion is Huntington disease. C: Lewy bodies are Parkinson disease. E: JC virus in oligodendrocytes causes PML.

questions.stem: A patient with Z-variant α1-antitrypsin develops cirrhosis. Which mechanism best explains the liver damage?

options.A: Loss of function: low plasma levels leave the liver unprotected
options.C: Toxic gain of function: polymers accumulate in hepatocytes
options.E: ER retention and ERAD of a protein that stays soluble

questions.explanation: Z-variant α1-antitrypsin misfolds and polymerizes in hepatocytes: a toxic gain of function that damages the liver, while its absence from plasma causes emphysema. A: Low plasma levels explain the lung disease, not the liver disease. B: Templated conversion is specific to prions. D: Missing M6P is I-cell disease. E: Retention and degradation without aggregation is ΔF508 CFTR (loss of function).

questions.stem: A patient's missense variant gives a high-confidence AlphaFold model with no visible change in the overall fold. What is the best conclusion?

options.A: It is benign, because the fold is preserved
options.B: It cannot be called benign on this basis
options.C: It is pathogenic, because AlphaFold models are static
options.D: It must lie in an intrinsically disordered region
options.E: The model is invalid for a single protein

questions.explanation: AlphaFold can't reliably predict how a point mutation affects stability or function; a variant can abolish catalysis, binding or trafficking without changing the fold, so conservation and functional data are still needed. A: A preserved fold doesn't mean preserved function. C: Being static is a limitation, not evidence of pathogenicity. D: Disordered regions are where AlphaFold is weak, so a high-confidence model argues against this. E: Single proteins are what AlphaFold predicts best.
